newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-South African tourists enjoy sea, safari -- and Soweto.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-South African tourists enjoy sea, safari -- and Soweto.

text.p: Violent crime may be putting foreigners off visiting South Africa, but those who do make it are flocking to one of the roughest places on earth -- Soweto.

Fresh from luxury resorts or national parks once reserved for whites, and shepherded by local guides, they venture warily into the crowded black city to see the "real" South Africa and perhaps to calm their consciences.
"You can wind the windows down, it's safe now," says a grinning Abraham Mofokeng, playing on the anxieties of his busload of tourists. "We've reached Soweto. Welcome."
Welcome to the township with a few million people -- no one knows how many -- and a crime rate second to none.
Welcome also to one of the new South Africa's fastest-growing tourist spots, a dusty sprawl of brick huts, shacks, street vendors and a sea of minibus taxis.
"Soweto was number one on my list," said 80-year-old Helen Merchant of Cincinnati.

Like most Soweto day trippers, who board their buses in downtown Johannesburg or its safer green suburbs, half an hour away over the hill, Mofokeng's guests are foreigners, Dutch, German, British, Australian.
They tut-tut indignantly as he recalls harsh apartheid laws that consigned blacks to shantytowns and choked their education, to stop them getting ideas above their station.
But there's also a quieter breed of tourist among the 100 or so daily minibus trippers these days.
"We're getting more and more white South Africans," said Jimmy Ntintili, who runs one of several rival companies doing the rounds of Soweto.

Most local whites would never have had the idea to visit in the apartheid days. Now, the murders, shootings, muggings and gunpoint carjackings keep them away. The tour guides retort that Johannesburg is no more relaxed.
Despite the bullet hole in Mofokeng's van, he says they have never had any trouble, people are safe with him.
The tour starts at a shared-taxi rank, whose rows of beat-up minibuses -- run by fierce rivals who frequently resort to shootouts over passengers -- are the only form of transport for most blacks.
The one bus full of white faces stands out.
Over the road, and past the curbside butchers, grocers and vendors who do much of Soweto's trade, is the compound where stolen vehicles line up as far as the eye can see.
Then it's off to see the homes of the poorest and the wealthiest in the township -- corrugated-iron squatter-camp shacks and the mansions of "Beverly Hills".
"This is Madame Mandela's home," Mofokeng says, pointing out where Winnie lives behind high walls and security cameras. Up the road is Archbishop Desmond Tutu's place, wrapped in electric fencing.

The "mansions" are impressive but can't compare with the villas and park-like gardens of once whites-only Johannesburg where Winnie's ex-husband Nelson, constrained by the security and lifestyle of a president, has moved to.
Visitors see how a homeowner can make a living by sub-letting his garage and yard to a dozen poorer families.

The average tour also takes in landmarks from the 1976 schools uprising that sped apartheid's end; a church that became a centre of black resistance; a shebeen (back-room bar), and a glimpse of grim migrant-worker hostels.
The country's momentous political changes of the last few years are not obvious here but can be seen in the newly tarred roads and new housing developments sprouting up.
At 100 rand ($21), the half-day trip costs as much as many Sowetans, those lucky enough to work, earn in a week.
Half a dozen operators now run the tours that began in the 1980s. Some are Sowetan entrepreneurs who have now moved into "Beverly Hills" themselves.
Soweto -- an abbreviation for South-Western Townships -- started life early this century as a labour compound.

When apartheid was introduced after World War Two, it became a convenient dumping ground for blacks expelled from areas of Johannesburg earmarked exclusively for whites. It was itself subdivided along black tribal lines.

The only whites living here run the power station that feeds Johannesburg. But two other whites are here -- former communist leader Joe Slovo and anti-apartheid activist Helen Joseph -- lying with the dead in Avalon cemetery.
Tourists, mostly white but with some black Americans, come away impressed by the good spirits and friendliness of the people, even those in shacks without water or power.
One Briton says he could not overcome feelings of guilt as he peered voyeuristically into the homes of the poor.

"We are not here to show you poverty -- I have seen worse poverty in Brazil -- but just to show you how the other half lives," said Ntintili, who calls his tour 'Soweto - the good, the bad and the ugly'.
The adventurous can now drink and dance the night away in shebeens on a Soweto-after-dark tour, or even stay in one of the city's handful of new bed and breakfasts.
Thoko Dube says that by opening her home, she is taking the Soweto experience a step further for outsiders who used just to peer from buses in the old days of state-run tours.
"This patronised the community and made tourists easy targets," the teacher said. "But now we can accommodate them and make them part of us, they are seen as friends."
